title: Own business and sole proprietorship
summary: The English rendering may narrow a reference to a worker's own business to a sole proprietorship. The legal and tax context has not yet established a different operative classification.

title: Federal rules and regulations
summary: A possible difference between federal rules and federal regulations needs more contextual review before it can be rated as a change in legal meaning.

title: “Twelve-year” bonus period
summary: The English twice says twelve years where Spanish says twelve months. The same English sentences expressly define an October-to-September year, so the review found no supported change to the operative measurement period.

title: Severance agreement and settlement agreement
summary: The 2017 tax-withholding amendment uses different agreement terms in Spanish and English. A targeted check of the original 2011 Code found its earlier §1062.01(a)(1)(G) bilingual wording aligned; that older text does not resolve the later amendment. Whether “settlement” excludes an agreement covered by the Spanish 2017 wording still requires period-specific tax-law review.

title: Notice of intended dismissal
summary: Spanish expressly refers to notice of an intention to dismiss before severance can be settled. English says notice of discharge, which may also mean advance notice of an impending dismissal. The review could not establish a different timing rule.

title: Fixed-term contract presumption
summary: Spanish says a qualifying fixed-term contract is presumed valid; English says it shall be considered valid. Nearby language permits a challenge based on renewal practices, so a conclusive English reading remains unproved.

title: Unemployment increase and hiring date
summary: The English preamble omits a Spanish post-Act-hire qualifier in its discussion of unemployment increases. The operative unemployment provisions do not support the broader legal-rights change suggested by that omission.

title: Punitive and compensatory damages
summary: A preamble sentence changes punitive damages to compensatory damages in English. Nearby English text and the operative provision still address punitive damages, so the review found no supported change in the remedy.

title: Abusive indignities and derogatory criticism
summary: Spanish vejámenes is broader than the English “derogatory criticisms.” The examples of conduct causing a worker to resign are nonexclusive, and English still covers humiliations through acts or words. A different eligibility rule has not been established.

title: Express future federal amendments
summary: Spanish expressly includes future amendments to the federal wage law; English only says it “has subsequently been amended.” The same sentence says the federal minimum wage applies automatically, and federal coverage independently constrains any frozen reading. No distinct wage outcome has been established.

title: Working-time definitions and hour limits
summary: The final Spanish clause concerns what counts as working hours or time; English instead names minimum hours and a maximum workweek. An earlier English phrase already mentions what working hours are, and the federal-law reference is broad. No separate incorporated rule has been established.

title: Neglect of compliance and reticence
summary: Spanish names neglect of compliance; English says a person is reticent in complying. Both versions also penalize anyone who violates the provision, likely covering negligent failures, so a distinct misdemeanor boundary has not been shown.

title: Quasi-legislative powers and quasi-legal powers
summary: Spanish transfers quasi-legislative powers; the operative English clause says quasi-legal powers. The English title and motives correctly identify quasi-legislative authority, and no delegated power has been shown to fall outside the transfer.

title: Daily overtime qualifier omitted
summary: Spanish identifies premium compensation for daily overtime, while English says overtime without “daily.” Both tie the preserved benefit to preexisting mandatory decrees, which have not been reviewed to establish a broader English entitlement.

title: Working mothers and nursing mothers
summary: Spanish guarantees the breastfeeding or milk-expression break to a nursing mother who requests it; English Section 8 says all working mothers who request it. The Act defines nursing mother, describes a specifically lactation-related break, requires supporting certification, and uses the narrower term in Section 10. The review has not identified a person treated differently after those provisions are read together.

title: Salary earned and salary paid in the possible fine
summary: Spanish refers to three times the salary the employee earns for each denied day; English says salary paid. Withheld pay could yield a lower literal English reference amount, but “salary paid for each day” may mean the daily wage rate, and both versions leave the fine discretionary and tied to harm. Without a supported distinct calculation or application, this remains a screening note rather than a published impact finding.

title: Original paragraph (11) already covers annuities
summary: Both original 2011 languages contain paragraph (b)(11) for annuities. Spanish then makes IVU-Loto prizes separate (b)(12), while English nests them at (b)(11)(A)(vi). Act 4 of 2017 later labels a new severance exclusion (11); intervening Code amendments were not reconstructed, so this original paragraph is not treated as the direct bilingual pair for that later addition.

title: Taxable premium portion and group life insurance
summary: Spanish identifies the otherwise taxable portion of a group-life insurance premium; English names group term life insurance. The definition’s cost/value language and express cross-reference to the premium tax rule likely narrow the English to the same component. Both originals also duplicate the subsection’s (3) number, so the paragraph is identified by its heading. No distinct tax treatment is established.

title: Original severance withholding clause aligns
summary: The targeted original Spanish and English clauses both exclude specified Act 80 indemnity or employer–employee severance pay from the definition of wages for withholding. This does not resolve the separate wording question raised by Act 4’s 2017 amendment to the clause.
